title: Building a Library
story: You've built useful code — validators, loggers, data structures. Now package them into a reusable LIBRARY. Other developers (and future you!) should be able to import your code and use it without reading the internals. A well-designed library has a clean public API, hidden implementation details, and works for everyone.
why: Libraries are the unit of code reuse — every `import` you've ever written was someone else's library; now you'll learn to design one that others would want to use.
analogy: A library is like a LEGO set — you provide standard bricks (types and functions) and connector specifications (interfaces). Users can build with your bricks, add their own custom bricks, and everything snaps together because of the standard connectors. A good library doesn't just solve one problem — it gives users the tools to solve problems you never imagined.
try_it: Expand the shapes library: add `Triangle` (area = base * height / 2), add `describe_shape` that returns a string description, and make Area extend into a bigger interface (`Measurable` with area AND perimeter). Then package a second library — a `validation` library with email and password validators. Notice how each library is a self-contained toolkit.
tips: Design your library around interfaces — concrete types come and go, but interfaces define the contract
Keep your public API small — every `pub` item is a promise you must keep; add sparingly
Test your library by USING it in a separate module — dogfooding reveals API flaws
common_mistakes: Exposing internal types as pub — if users start depending on your internals, you can't change them later
Making a library that only works with the author's types — a good library lets users plug in their OWN types via interfaces
Publishing a library without documentation — `pub` items need clear names and purposes since users can't see the source
